reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Endocrine Society
clinicalPearls: A surgically curable cause of secondary hypertension in which an adrenal adenoma autonomously secretes aldosterone
Should be suspected in hypertension that is resistant, of early onset, or accompanied by unexplained or diuretic-induced hypokalaemia, though many patients are normokalaemic
Screening uses the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, which shows high aldosterone with suppressed renin activity
A raised ratio is confirmed with a dynamic test demonstrating failure of aldosterone to suppress with sodium or volume loading
Adrenal vein sampling is the key step to distinguish a unilateral aldosterone source (adenoma) from bilateral adrenal hyperplasia before recommending surgery
Aldosterone excess causes sodium retention, potassium and hydrogen loss, and a metabolic alkalosis alongside the hypertension
Unilateral disease may be cured or markedly improved by adrenalectomy, whereas bilateral disease is managed medically with mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists
Aldosterone excess causes cardiovascular and renal damage beyond that explained by blood pressure alone, so identification and treatment matter
reference.pathophysiology: An aldosterone-producing adenoma is a benign adrenocortical tumour of the zona glomerulosa that secretes aldosterone independently of the renin-angiotensin system. Autonomous aldosterone drives distal nephron sodium reabsorption in exchange for potassium and hydrogen ions, expanding extracellular volume and producing hypertension, hypokalaemia, and metabolic alkalosis. The volume expansion suppresses renin. Somatic mutations in ion channels and transporters (such as KCNJ5) are frequently found in these adenomas and promote calcium-dependent aldosterone synthesis and cell proliferation. Chronic mineralocorticoid excess also exerts direct pro-fibrotic effects on the heart, vasculature, and kidney.
additionalDifferentials: Essential hypertension with hypokalaemia from diuretics
Glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism and other familial hyperaldosteronism
Cushing syndrome and apparent mineralocorticoid excess
additionalInvestigations: Aldosterone-to-renin ratio as the screening test, with attention to interfering medications
Confirmatory suppression testing (oral sodium loading or saline infusion)
Serum potassium, bicarbonate, and acid-base assessment
Adrenal CT to characterise adrenal morphology
Adrenal vein sampling to lateralise aldosterone production before surgery
redFlags: Severe hypokalaemia causing muscle weakness, arrhythmia, or paralysis
Accelerated or malignant hypertension with end-organ damage
Marked metabolic alkalosis with cardiac irritability requiring urgent correction
reference.prognosis: Unilateral adenoma treated with adrenalectomy often cures or substantially improves hypertension and corrects hypokalaemia; medical therapy with mineralocorticoid receptor blockade controls disease when surgery is not appropriate, and early treatment reduces excess cardiovascular and renal risk.
pitfalls: Interpreting the aldosterone-to-renin ratio without accounting for interfering drugs and potassium status
Proceeding to surgery on CT appearances alone without adrenal vein sampling to confirm lateralisation
Attributing an incidental adrenal nodule to be the functional source when hyperplasia is bilateral
Under-recognising primary aldosteronism as a common and treatable cause of resistant hypertension
